cards.title: Police at school gates
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: This story addresses important issues of governance, human rights, education policy, and youth welfare in Pakistan.
cards.summary: The Punjab government plans to search students' bags at school gates to stop vaping and substance abuse. However, the editorial criticizes using the Crime Control Department (CCD) for this task. The CCD has a reputation for human rights abuses and extrajudicial killings. The editorial argues that educators, not police, should handle student discipline, and law enforcement should focus on suppliers of illicit substances.
key_facts: The Punjab government decided to search students' bags at educational institutions.
The Crime Control Department (CCD) was established last year.
The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) accused the CCD of extrajudicial killings.
Petitions in the Lahore High Court cited allegations of illegal detentions and misconduct by the CCD.

vocab.meaning: deserving strong disapproval
outside of legal process, without legal authority
treated as if shameful or disgraced

text: Curbing the rise of vaping and substance abuse among youth is an urgent necessity. Thus, the Punjab government's decision to search students' bags outside educational institutions across the province is commendable in intent, yet what is condemnable is the use of the Crime Control Department (CCD) - a specialised crime-fighting police unit - to ensure students do not carry cigarettes, vapes and other intoxicating substances. This is all the more troubling because the CCD has earned a fearsome reputation in just over a year of existence, having been set up only last year. Human rights bodies, including the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP), have accused it of extrajudicial killings and bypassing due process. Furthermore, petitions in the Lahore High Court have cited allegations of illegal detentions and misconduct. Disciplining students inside academic spaces should be the job of educators themselves, not police. Routine checks can easily be handled by class teachers, student proctors or school administrators without turning campus gates into security checkpoints. It goes without saying that subjecting teenagers and pre-teens to searches by an infamous police wing carries psychological consequences. Treating adolescents like hardened suspects runs the risk of eroding their trust in authority and fostering resentment rather than genuine behavioural change. Instead of feeling safe in spaces meant for learning, children may feel intimidated, humiliated and stigmatised. To genuinely protect students from substance abuse, the authorities must tackle the problem at its root. First, law enforcement should focus on prosecuting shopkeepers and illicit networks selling vapes and narcotics near campuses. Second, institutions must introduce confidential counseling and awareness workshops led by psychologists. A drug-free campus is built through mentorship, parental engagement and supply-side enforcement - never through the heavy hand of a feared police force.

cards.title: Climate failure
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: Climate change is a critical global issue and a recurring essay topic, highlighting international policy failures and economic conflicts.
cards.summary: Global climate talks are failing because countries prioritize economic interests over environmental protection. COP31 in Antalya collapsed after the European Union rejected a draft agreement. The main disagreement was over acknowledging fossil fuels as the primary cause of global warming. Oil-producing nations resisted phasing out fossil fuels, promoting costly carbon-removal technologies instead.
key_facts: Global climate diplomacy has reached a point of prioritizing economic interests.
COP31 in Antalya collapsed due to the rejection of a final draft agreement.
The European Union and several other countries rejected the agreement.
World leaders could not agree on acknowledging fossil fuels as primary drivers of global warming.
Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing countries resisted language threatening their petroleum economies.
The draft promoted carbon-removal technologies as a solution.

vocab.meaning: a wide gap or difference
causing or likely to cause an argument
making less severe or serious

text: Global climate diplomacy has reached a point where governments appear more determined to protect their economic interests than to preserve the planet's future. The collapse of COP31 in Antalya, following the rejection of a final draft agreement by the European Union and several other countries, has exposed the widening gulf between international climate pledges and the political will required to honour them. After more than two weeks of negotiations, world leaders could not even agree on acknowledging fossil fuels as the principal drivers of global warming. That such a fundamental scientific reality remains politically contentious speaks volumes about the sincerity of international climate commitments. At the centre of the disagreement was a draft that removed explicit references to transitioning away from fossil fuels while promoting carbon-removal technologies as a means of addressing rising temperatures. Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing countries reportedly resisted language that would threaten their petroleum-dependent economies. Carbon capture undoubtedly has a role in mitigating emissions, but treating an expensive and insufficiently scalable technology as a substitute for reducing fossil fuel consumption risks perpetuating the very practices responsible for the crisis. Equally questionable is the moral position adopted by wealthy industrialised nations. The EU's refusal to endorse an agreement devoid of meaningful fossil fuel commitments may be justified, but its environmental convictions must also be measured against its own energy policies. European governments continue to support fossil fuel investments even as they demand greater ambition from developing economies. Rejecting an inadequate agreement is preferable to endorsing one that legitimises inaction. However, rejection alone cannot constitute climate leadership. Wealthy countries must demonstrate consistency between their domestic energy policies and international demands. Most importantly, climate finance must cease being a bargaining instrument and become a dependable commitment.

cards.title: Terrorism and preparedness
cards.author: Dr Syed Akhtar Ali Shah
cards.why: This article directly addresses critical issues of terrorism, internal security, governance challenges, and resource management in Pakistan.
cards.summary: A recent armed attack in Kohat's Gumbat tehsil, where ten police personnel were martyred, highlights the erosion of state authority in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. This incident, linked to illegal placer-gold mining, suggests a nexus between illicit miners and militant networks. The author questions the operational preparedness of the police, including intelligence gathering, terrain assessment, and planning for hostile environments. He stresses the need to examine why such violence persists.
key_facts: An armed attack occurred on November 11 at Darbukach in Kohat's Gumbat tehsil.
Ten police personnel were martyred in the attack.
Police reported killing eighteen assailants.
The attack followed incidents at Speen Mela Police Post, Bannu's Gumbati checkpost, and a Karak ambush.
Illegal placer-gold mining operates along the Indus, from Kund and Khairabad towards Shakardarra.
Police allege a nexus between illicit miners and militants in Kohat.

vocab.meaning: the gradual destruction or reduction of something
a connection or series of connections linking two or more things
a place or position affording a good view or advantage

text: The November 11 armed attack on a police contingent at Darbukach in Kohat's Gumbat tehsil portrays a disturbing picture of the erosion of the writ of the state in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Reports emanating from different sources indicate that ten police personnel were martyred while returning from an operation against illegal placer-gold mining. Police also reported killing eighteen assailants. This loss follows attacks on the Speen Mela Police Post at Hassan Khel, Bannu's Gumbati checkpost, and a Karak ambush that claimed the lives of four policemen. Praising the valour and sense of duty of the fallen is necessary to keep motivating the force engaged against terrorism, yet it remains insufficient. Their sacrifice makes it all the more urgent to examine why such violence persists. Gold deposits along the Indus, from Kund and Khairabad towards Shakardarra, should have been a gift of God for local communities and a boost to the provincial economy. Unfortunately, that belt has been swarmed by armed gangs busy in illegal extraction, reportedly with the support of militant networks. Areas rich in natural resources appear to have been turned into a proverbial "Wild West", where these groups impose their will at gunpoint. The police themselves allege a nexus between illicit miners and militants in Kohat. Given such lethal retaliation, enforcing mining laws now extends far beyond ordinary mineral regulation. The incident also brings the issue of operational preparedness to the fore. Was adequate intelligence obtained about the adversaries and their capacity? Was the surrounding terrain, including possible vantage points, properly assessed? Were withdrawal routes, communications, reinforcements and casualty evacuation planned for a hostile environment? Was it anticipated that, in such an eventuality, the force might encounter a more sophisticated militant threat? Yet without an independent, professional inquiry, these possibilities cannot be treated as established facts. The objective of posing these questions is to improve training, equipment, command arrangements and officer safety - not to diminish the courage of those who died. Another dangerous aspect is the shadowy economy it sustains. Violent non-state actors can gain access to mining, mint money, control transport, influence mineral markets and nurture relationships with people whose livelihoods have become dependent upon illegal activity. Some residents may view them as providers of income or dispute resolution; others may submit out of fear. Both circumstances weaken intelligence gathering, encourage recruitment and sustain militant finances. The government must, therefore, go after not just the gunmen, but also the financiers, buyers, suppliers, facilitators and anyone else who protects these illegal operations. The reported task given to the Area Representative and Development Council to engage with militants raises another serious concern. At a press conference on November 11, a spokesperson for the Council, quoting the Prime Minister, said that militancy could vanish from the twelve disturbed districts forever within three months if council members and residents persuaded militants to leave. But what does "leave" mean? Would militants lay down their weapons, renounce violence and live in accordance with the law? Or would they simply move to greener pastures, cross the border or regroup? Shifting them elsewhere cannot eliminate the threat, nor does it constitute a lasting restoration of state authority. My own experience serving in conflict zones in senior police and administrative positions, reinforced by research for my PhD thesis, "Fault Lines of Governance: Challenges of Militancy and Extremism in Pakistan", suggests that comparable measures have not produced the desired results in the past. Tribal elders may be effective in mediating disputes of a local nature, but they cannot be expected to neutralise organised armed movements. Indeed, the South Asia Terrorism Portal recorded at least 194 tribal elders killed in 143 incidents between 2005 and early March 2024. Many were targeted for standing with the government. To expose their successors to similar risks without enforceable protection is to ignore this tragic history. The 2022 negotiations - followed by the TTP ceasefire - which involved tribal elders, failed to yield the dividends of peace. Demands regarding the withdrawal of security forces and the reversal of FATA's merger became major obstacles. Dialogue and peace agreements are not inherently objectionable, but their terms and conditions must be unambiguous, and in no case should they appear to be a surrender of the writ of the state. The mandate, safeguards, verification mechanisms and consequences for non-compliance must be clearly defined. Political scientist Francis Fukuyama's concept of "stateness first" is relevant here. Following 9/11, he emphasised that weak institutions result in disorder and the proliferation of transnational security threats. Yet stateness means the capacity to enforce legitimate laws and deliver basic public goods, not arbitrary coercion. Governance ultimately concerns citizens' security, justice, welfare and ability to live without fear. Ideological extremism, including the selective misuse of religious narratives to legitimise violence, must be challenged; however, security operations alone cannot fill the institutional vacuums in which armed groups thrive. The response must combine intelligence-led policing, a capable Counter-Terrorism Department, sound investigations and credible prosecutions with decisive action against illicit mining and militant financing. Transparent licensing, environmental safeguards and legitimate employment can help detach communities from the underground economy. In the merged districts, meaningful administrative and judicial integration must be matched by adequate financial resources. The announced special funding for police capacity and anti-drone systems should translate into measurable protection on the ground. Furthermore, the government should publish verifiable data on attacks, extortion, kidnappings, illegal mining, prosecutions and civilian safety. The true measure of the writ of the state lies not in temporary clearance operations, casualty counts or promises that militants will depart within three months. Its real test is whether citizens can travel, work, attend school and obtain justice without seeking permission from armed groups. In essence, the duty to ensure the security and freedom of citizens belongs solely to the state; it cannot be delegated to vulnerable elders.

cards.title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
cards.author: Michael C. Desch
cards.why: This analysis is highly relevant for Current Affairs, International Relations, and understanding peace efforts in major global conflicts.
cards.summary: The article suggests it's time to negotiate a settlement with Russia regarding the Ukraine war. It references former US President Donald Trump's eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin, temporarily pausing sanctions. While Trump framed this as a move to keep Russia at the bargaining table, the author notes it also aimed to bolster the US economy. The author argues that concessions like the fuel deal could genuinely move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace.
key_facts: US President Donald Trump secured a deal for diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin in October.
The deal involved pausing sanctions imposed by Trump's own administration.
Trump described the arrangement as a way to keep Russia at 'the bargaining table'.
Trump reportedly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The article suggests such concessions could move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace.

vocab.meaning: a maneuver or tactic to gain an advantage
supporting or strengthening
opposed to liberal principles or policies, especially regarding individual rights

text: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

cards.title: Musadik's Delhi moment
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: This story offers insights into Pakistan-India relations, diplomatic challenges, and regional forums like the SCO.
cards.summary: Pakistan's Federal Minister for Climate Change, Dr Musadik Malik, faced hostile questioning from Indian media during an SCO Civilizational Dialogue forum in New Delhi. The editorial praised Dr Malik for his calm and articulate responses amidst the belligerent atmosphere. This visit was the first high-level engagement in over three years, following worsened diplomatic ties due to incidents like the Pahalgam attack in April 2025 and a military confrontation in May 2025. Despite the challenges, Dr Malik expressed hope for future bilateral dialogue.
key_facts: Federal Minister for Climate Change Dr Musadik Malik visited New Delhi for the SCO Civilizational Dialogue forum.
The visit was the first high-level engagement between Pakistan and India in over three years.
Then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended a similar SCO moot in Goa in May 2023.
Diplomatic ties worsened after the Pahalgam attack in April 2025.
A four-day military confrontation occurred in May 2025.
Dr Malik stated any dialogue on 'terrorism' must be 'based on evidence'.

vocab.meaning: aggressive or warlike behavior
a sharp, quick, or witty reply
excessive pride or self-confidence

text: The SCO Civilizational Dialogue forum held in New Delhi will long be remembered for bullying a guest from Pakistan. Federal Minister for Climate Change Dr Musadik Malik faced relentless attempts to grill him by the Indian media on every issue on earth, except the subject for which he was there. That spoke of the belligerence in the air and the level of intolerance that has crept into the Indian media. Kudos to Dr Malik for keeping his cool while engaging a hostile audience with his bilingual retort, which also featured poetry to lighten the mood. He exhibited his articulation by confining himself to the bare minimum of words while responding to provocative questions. The minister was apt when he said any dialogue between Pakistan and India on "terrorism" must be "based on evidence," resting his country's case on reason. Dr Malik's three-day official visit came after a break of more than three years, since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari toured Goa to participate in a similar SCO moot in May 2023. Later, the Pahalgam attack of April 2025 led to a further downgrading of diplomatic ties, with high-level engagement entirely absent since the arch-foes engaged in a four-day military confrontation in May 2025. With diplomatic relations at their lowest ebb and consular facilitation non-existent, it was a rare opportunity for India to extend due courtesy to its high-profile guest from Pakistan and kick-start a new episode of meaningful interaction. That was sadly not the case, as vendetta and hubris ruled the roost. Dr Malik, nonetheless, was able to make some strides as he expressed hope that bilateral dialogue would resume at the earliest. He was spot-on when he said he would prefer to answer loaded queries concerning interstate ties at an opportune moment when specifically called upon to do so. That was clarity at work, intended not to stir any unnecessary controversy. His remarks must serve as a preamble for a meaningful dialogue on climate change: "GLOFs and glaciers are blind, they do not know whether to fall on the right or the left." That is the evolving shared threat that both neighbours must confront immediately.

cards.title: Why don't we protest?
cards.author: Akbar N Shad
cards.why: This analysis delves into societal behavior, democratic participation, and civil society, which are important for Pakistan Affairs and Governance.
cards.summary: The author questions why Pakistani society is reluctant to protest unfair situations, illustrated by an incident on public transport. Unlike young people in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, and India who frequently protest, collective resistance in Pakistan seems limited. The piece speculates on the reasons, including a colonial legacy of obedience and the role of civil society.
key_facts: The author observed reluctance to protest among public transport users.
Young people in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, and India actively protest.
Generation Z in these countries brings public concerns into the political mainstream.

vocab.meaning: unwilling or hesitant
formal complaints or reasons for protest
lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern

text: A seemingly minor incident during my daily commute to the office recently set me thinking about a much larger question: Why have we, as a society, become so reluctant to protest? I was travelling in a coaster van that operates on a pre-booking system and charges more than twice the fare of ordinary public transport. On this particular day, all seats in the coach were occupied. However, at one of the stops, a youngster boarded. He was a regular traveller on the same service and must have known that he had been given a pass even after all the seats had been booked and that the back seat had room for only four people. Yet he chose to quietly squeeze himself between the others in the back seat rather than raising his voice against the irregularity. His action disturbed the comfort of everyone seated there. Interestingly, when I protested nobody came to my support. The incident was trivial in itself, but it raised a question that has continued to trouble me. Why did the fifth passenger not protest and why did the others accept an arrangement that was plainly unfair? The question becomes even more relevant when we look at developments across South Asia. In Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and India, young people, particularly members of Generation Z, have taken to the streets to express their grievances and demand change. Their protests have, in different ways and with varying outcomes, brought public concerns into the political mainstream. Yet in Pakistan, where everyday life offers no shortage of reasons for discontent, collective resistance often appears limited. Why don't we protest? Or to be more exact, why does only an insignificant portion of our people take to the streets when push comes to shove? Is it a legacy of our colonial past, when obedience to authority was cultivated and dissent discouraged? Have generations of living under hierarchical systems taught us to accept decisions rather than question them? Or is it the result of a political environment in which people often fear the consequences of speaking out? Pakistan's political and institutional landscape has, at times, made dissent a difficult undertaking. Concerns about pressure, restrictions and the personal cost of challenging authority can discourage ordinary citizens from raising their voices. For those without influence, resources or access to powerful circles, even a small act of resistance may appear risky. There is also a deeply rooted tendency in our society to wait for circumstances to change on their own - a tendency that Christina Lamb has phrased as "Waiting for Allah". Many people respond to injustice, delays and disappointments by invoking maslehat - the belief that there may be a larger divine purpose behind events. Faith can provide comfort and strength, but it should not become an excuse for accepting avoidable injustice or abandoning our responsibility to improve our circumstances. Marx's description of faith as the "opium of the people" is often cited in discussions about how belief can be used to discourage questioning. But the issue is not faith itself; it is the use of fatalism to normalise conditions that people have the ability and right to challenge. Spiritual conviction and civic responsibility need not be in conflict. Protest does not necessarily mean confrontation or disorder. It can begin with a simple objection to an unfair practice, a demand for one's lawful rights or the collective insistence that rules be followed. But a society that cannot object to the unfair treatment meted out by a transport operator will find it difficult to challenge much greater injustices.

cards.author: Emily Kilcrease, Vivek Chilukuri
cards.why: This topic is crucial for understanding global technology rivalry and its implications for national security and international trade.

cards.title: Burmah Oil: burned by its own government
cards.author: Haroon Rashid Siddiqi
cards.why: This historical account provides valuable context on colonial economic practices, resource exploitation, and the origins of major energy companies, relevant to Pakistan Affairs and economic history.
cards.summary: The Burmah Oil Company, founded in 1886 by David Sime Cargill, evolved from traditional Burmese oil extraction into a major British Empire petroleum firm. It financed oil exploration in Persia, leading to the creation of Anglo-Persian Oil (later BP), and expanded its operations in India. During World War II in 1942, British authorities ordered Burmah Oil engineers to destroy their own facilities to prevent them from falling into Japanese hands. The company's legacy also extended to Pakistan.
key_facts: Burmese people extracted oil along the Irrawaddy in Yenangyaung for centuries.
David Sime Cargill founded the Burmah Oil Company in Glasgow in 1886.
Burmah Oil financed William Knox D'Arcy's search for oil in Persia, leading to Anglo-Persian Oil Company (later BP).
The company took over the Assam Oil Company and operated the Digboi oilfield.
Burmah Oil joined with Shell in a venture known as Burmah-Shell.
In early 1942, British authorities ordered the destruction of Burmah Oil facilities in Burma to deny them to advancing Japanese forces.

vocab.meaning: took control of (a territory or country)
passed down from generation to generation
to completely destroy

text: Along the banks of the Irrawaddy, in the dusty plains of Yenangyaung, the people of Burma had been extracting oil from the earth for centuries. The wells were hand-dug, narrow and deep, and belonged to hereditary families. The crude was used in lamps, while a coating of oil protected wooden boats against water and decay. Few could have foreseen that this modest local trade would eventually become an important part of the petroleum industry of the British Empire. In 1886, a year after the British annexed Upper Burma and sent King Thibaw into exile, a Scottish merchant named David Sime Cargill founded the Burmah Oil Company in Glasgow. Mechanised operations gradually replaced traditional methods, a refinery was established at Syriam near Rangoon, and kerosene began finding markets across the subcontinent. Burmah Oil grew into one of Asia's major oil companies. Its interests extended well beyond Burma. The company financed William Knox D'Arcy's search for oil in Persia, an undertaking that led to the establishment of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later known as BP. In India, Burmah Oil took over the Assam Oil Company in stages, eventually operating through it the historic Digboi oilfield. It also joined hands with Shell in a petroleum marketing venture known as Burmah-Shell. The company's influence extended to Pakistan as well, leaving a legacy that persists today. By early 1942, Japanese forces had overrun Malaya and Singapore and were advancing into Burma. The British authorities were determined not to allow the Japanese war machine to take possession of the country's oil resources. Burmah Oil's engineers were instructed to demolish the very facilities they had spent years developing. Wells were plugged, pumps disabled, storage tanks destroyed and refineries demolished, extensively damaging the oilfields of Yenangyaung and Chauk. When the Japanese occupied the area, the infrastructure had been rendered unusable, frustrating their war effort. Burmah Oil had complied with the British government's wartime requirements, but the question of compensation proved far more contentious. After the war, the company and associated claimants sought compensation exceeding £31 million for property destroyed at the government's direction. The postwar response was inadequate: the British government provided approximately £4.75 million from a wider allocation of £10 million for rehabilitation, but refused to meet the balance of the claims. Maintaining that it was entitled to compensation under the law, the company took the Crown to court. Since the company was headquartered in Glasgow, proceedings were brought in Scotland against the Lord Advocate. A Scottish judge initially ruled in the claimants' favour, but the senior judges of the Court of Session in Edinburgh reversed the decision. Burmah Oil then appealed to the House of Lords. For readers in the subcontinent, it is worth explaining the unusual position occupied by the House of Lords in the British constitutional system. It was the upper chamber of Parliament, comprising members mostly without legal qualifications, but until 2009 it also served as Britain's highest court of appeal through a small group of senior judges known as the Law Lords. On 21 April 1964, the Law Lords decided the Burmah Oil case by a majority of three to two, holding that the destruction of the company's installations, although lawful as a wartime measure, gave rise to a right to compensation. The company had secured a significant legal victory before Britain's highest court. The victory was short-lived. Harold Wilson's government was alarmed by the possible financial consequences and substantial Treasury liabilities if other claimants sought similar payments. There was no higher court to appeal to, so Parliament intervened. In 1965, Parliament passed the War Damage Act, retrospectively abolishing the common-law right to compensation for property damaged or destroyed by lawful acts of the Crown during wartime, applying it even to proceedings already under way. The legislation removed the legal foundation of Burmah Oil's claim, preventing the company from securing the practical benefit of its victory. The episode remains a striking example of the limits of judicial protection against retrospective legislation when government finances are threatened. Burmah Oil's financial fortunes subsequently took a dramatic turn. By the mid-1970s, heavy losses in its tanker business and an American oil acquisition - financed partly through borrowing against its BP shareholding - brought the company close to collapse amidst falling tanker rates and a sharp decline in BP's share price. The Bank of England intervened in January 1975 by purchasing Burmah Oil's BP shares to prevent a disorderly failure. Burmah subsequently reorganised its business around Castrol, the lubricants company acquired in 1966, becoming Burmah-Castrol before being acquired in 2000 by BP Amoco. Its Pakistan interests had passed into Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL), established in 1950 with Burmah Oil as its major shareholder. PPL went on to discover the vast Sui gas field in 1952, an event of lasting importance to Pakistan's energy sector. The history of Burmah Oil deserves to be remembered for more than its contribution to the petroleum industry of Burma, India and Pakistan. It built an extensive business, destroyed its own installations at the British government's direction during the Second World War, and spent years pursuing compensation through the courts. Even after obtaining a favourable judgment from Britain's highest court, it found that Parliament could deprive it of the practical benefit of its victory. The company was expected to make the sacrifice when the government required it, but was left to bear much of the loss when the war was over. It is a reminder that the interests of the state and the rights of those who serve its purposes do not always coincide.

cards.title: No longer curious
cards.author: Muhammad Hamid Zaman
cards.why: This piece highlights critical issues in higher education and research, relevant for discussions on education reform and national development.
cards.summary: The author expresses concern that curiosity is diminishing in academic research. Research is becoming transactional, focusing on outputs like papers and degrees rather than genuine inquiry. Universities are investing in programs with short-term financial returns or popularity fads, neglecting those that foster deep thinking. This trend reduces creativity and discourages students from pursuing new questions.

vocab.meaning: relating to an exchange or interaction, often for a specific outcome
following a set of rules or steps
a difficult problem or riddle
